L28@P0: This paper presents a novel integrated approach for efficient optimization based online trajectory
L29@P0: planning of topologically distinctive mobile robot trajectories. Online trajectory optimization deforms an
L30@P0: initial coarse path generated by a global planner by minimizing objectives such as path length, transition
L31@P0: time or control effort. Kinodynamic motion properties of mobile robots and clearance from obstacles
L32@P0: impose additional equality and inequality constraints on the trajectory optimization. Local planners
L33@P0: account for efficiency by restricting the search space to locally optimal solutions only. However, the
L34@P0: objective function is usually non-convex as the presence of obstacles generates multiple distinctive local
L35@P0: optima.
L36@P0: The proposed method maintains and simultaneously optimizes a subset of admissible candidate
L37@P0: trajectories of distinctive topologies and thus seeking the overall best candidate among the set of
L38@P0: alternative local solutions. Time-optimal trajectories for differential-drive and carlike robots are obtained
L39@P0: efficiently by adopting the Timed-Elastic-Band approach for the underlying trajectory optimization problem. The investigation of various example scenarios and a comparative analysis with conventional local
L40@P0: planners confirm the advantages of integrated exploration, maintenance and optimization of topologically
L41@P0: distinctive trajectories.

L43@P0: 1. Introduction
L44@P0: In the context of service robotics and autonomous transportation systems, mobile robots are required to navigate in highly
L45@P0: dynamic environments while accomplishing complex tasks. On
L46@P0: this occasion, one of the fundamental challenges in mobile robotics
L47@P0: is concerned with the development of universally applicable motion planning strategies. Online planning is preferred over offline
L48@P0: approaches since they immediately respond to changes in the
L49@P0: environment or perturbations of the robot motion at runtime. The
L50@P0: well known elastic band approach [1] locally deforms a path online.

L54@P0: Predefined internal forces contract the path while external forces
L55@P0: maintain a separation from obstacles. An alternative established
L56@P0: path planning approach based on an optimization technique is
L57@P0: presented in [2]. However, conventional path planning does not
L58@P0: explicitly incorporate temporal and (kino-)dynamic aspects of motion, therefore ignoring constraints imposed by kinematic or dynamic motion models with bounded velocities and accelerations.
L59@P0: Kurniawati et al. extend the elastic band approach to the online
L60@P0: deformation of trajectories rather than paths [3]. The approach
L61@P0: consists of two stages that at first repel discrete trajectory points
L62@P0: from obstacles and secondly enforce connectedness w.r.t. a dynamic motion model. Delsart et al. combine both stages into a
L63@P0: single operation [4].

L66@P1: Trajectory optimization usually attempts to minimize either
L67@P1: control effort, control error or the transition time between start
L68@P1: and goal pose. However, the computational burden required to
L69@P1: find an optimal solution is high, which limits its direct online
L70@P1: integration with feedback control. Due to this observation many
L71@P1: researchers are focusing on obtaining solutions or even approximations of the underlying trajectory optimization problem efficiently. The dynamic window approach (DWA) constitutes a
L72@P1: widely applied method for mobile robot navigation [5]. Simulated
L73@P1: trajectories are sampled repeatedly from a velocity search space
L74@P1: restricted by a set of feasible velocities. A cost function evaluates
L75@P1: each candidate trajectory w.r.t. the remaining distance to the goal,
L76@P1: the forward velocity and separation from obstacles. The lowestcost solution is selected for controlling the robot. The approach
L77@P1: accounts for efficiency by restricting the feasible set of valid trajectories to a subset of sampled candidates with segments of constant
L78@P1: velocity leading to merely suboptimal trajectories. Lau et al. [6]
L79@P1: and Sprunk et al. [7] optimize trajectories represented by splines
L80@P1: continuously according to kinodynamic constraints of the robot.
L81@P1: An online planning algorithm that relies on a covariant gradient
L82@P1: descent method is presented in [8]. In a previous work the authors
L83@P1: present a further extension to the elastic band called Timed-ElasticBand (TEB) approach [9,10]. The TEB efficiently optimizes the robot
L84@P1: trajectory w.r.t. (kino-)dynamic constraints and non-holonomic
L85@P1: kinematics while explicitly incorporating temporal information
L86@P1: in order to reach the goal pose in minimal time. The approach
L87@P1: accounts for efficiency by exploiting the sparsity structure of the
L88@P1: underlying problem formulation. It has been generalized to an efficient time-optimal model predictive control approach for dynamic
L89@P1: systems [11].
L90@P1: In practice, due to limited computational resources online optimization is usually performed using local optimization techniques
L91@P1: for which the discovery of the global optimal trajectory is not
L92@P1: guaranteed. Especially in mobile robot navigation local minima
L93@P1: often emerge due to the presence of obstacles. Kalakrishnan et al.
L94@P1: apply a stochastic descent method to partially overcome these limitations [12]. However, the approach requires extensive sampling
L95@P1: of trajectories in order to estimate the true gradient w.r.t. the global
L96@P1: optimum. A two stage local optimization approach that generates a
L97@P1: set of alternative, topologically distinctive trajectories is presented
L98@P1: by Kuderer et al. [13]. The proposed method extracts multiple
L99@P1: candidate trajectories from a modified Voronoi diagram that often
L100@P1: coincide with the local minima of the optimization problem. Paths
L101@P1: that belong to the same equivalence class are grouped by an equivalence relation based on the winding number at each obstacle. The
L102@P1: paper at hand pursues a related approach for filtering distinctive
L103@P1: candidate trajectories in the context of online trajectory planning.
L104@P1: It mainly differs from [13] w.r.t. sampling strategy, equivalence
L105@P1: relation and the trajectory optimization technique.
L106@P1: The idea of exploring topologically distinctive paths and trajectories is not novel. However, past approaches mainly focus on
L107@P1: global offline path and trajectory planning. Probabilistic roadmap
L108@P1: (PRM) methods that operate with different equivalence relations
L109@P1: are presented in [14] and [15]. The proposed algorithms are in
L110@P1: principle able to identify complicated paths in large, complex
L111@P1: environments but rely upon an algorithmic rather than closed form
L112@P1: computation of the equivalence relations. Our approach employs a
L113@P1: computationally more efficient sampling strategy and equivalence
L114@P1: relation. It is intended to operate in a local subregion of the environment and is thus suited for online trajectory optimization.
L115@P1: Obviously, this does not replace the need for global planning in
L116@P1: large environments. Knepper et al. propose a local planner based
L117@P1: on path sampling and the Hausdorff metric as equivalence relation [16]. The planner performs a discrete path selection rather
L118@P1: than deforming continuous trajectories. An equivalence relation
L119@P1: originating from the field of complex analysis is presented by
L120@P1: Fig. 1. TEB trajectory representation with n = 3 poses.
L121@P1: Bhattacharya et al. [17]. The closed form solution motivates its
L122@P1: application within our approach for trajectory filtering. Pokorny
L123@P1: et al. presents a graph free sampling based approach based on
L124@P1: filtrations of simplicial complexes [18].
L125@P1: This contribution presents an integrated online trajectory planning approach that combines the exploration and simultaneous
L126@P1: optimization of multiple admissible topologically distinctive trajectories during runtime. As an extended version of [19] the online
L127@P1: exploration strategy is fully integrated with the TEB approach
L128@P1: providing the underlying trajectory optimization. Hence the TEB
L129@P1: approach is entirely reformulated w.r.t. its original description [9]
L130@P1: and further extended to a more generic obstacle representation,
L131@P1: supporting forward and backward robot motion and to accomplish
L132@P1: navigation tasks for carlike robots beyond the differential-drive
L133@P1: robots considered in the original proposal. The combined and integrated approach preserves the locally optimal trajectory of each
L134@P1: equivalence class to facilitate warm starting from previous solutions. Candidate trajectories are sampled repeatedly and evolve
L135@P1: not only over space but also time which significantly reduces the
L136@P1: number of samples. The sample based approach is compared with
L137@P1: the systematic generation of waypoints from Voronoi diagrams regarding completeness of candidate trajectories and computational
L138@P1: efficiency. The presented approach is available as open-source C++
L139@P1: code and integrated into ROS [20].
L140@P1: The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 formulates the
L141@P1: local TEB optimization approach followed by the exploration of
L142@P1: trajectories in distinctive topologies in Section 3. The overall integration of exploration, planning and maintenance of trajectories
L143@P1: is described in Section 4. Section 5 demonstrates and evaluates
L144@P1: results obtained from realistic simulations with a differential drive
L145@P1: and a carlike mobile robot. The integrated planning approach is
L146@P1: compared with the original locally operating TEB and the DWA as
L147@P1: mentioned above. Finally, Section 6 summarizes the results and
L148@P1: provides an outlook on future work.

L375@P3: 2.3. Approximative least-squares optimization
L376@P3: Solving nonlinear programs with hard constraints is computational expensive. Therefore, improving the efficiency of fast online solvers has become an important research topic over the
L377@P3: last decade. The TEB approach further investigates the application of unconstrained optimization techniques since they are well
L378@P3: studied and mature implementations in open-source packages
L379@P3: are widely available. Unconstrained optimization avoids Lagrange
L380@P3: resp. Karush–Kuhn–Tucker multipliers (dual variables) causing the
L381@P3: dimension of the Hessian matrices to become identical with the
L382@P3: number of primal variables in b.
